title: 3 John

stories.title: 📜 3 John
summaryBullets: The elder, To the beloved Gaius, whom I love in the truth: (1:1).
Beloved, I pray that in every way you may prosper and enjoy good health, as your soul also prospers. (1:2).
For I was overjoyed when the brothers came and testified about your devotion to the truth, in which you continue to walk. (1:3).
I have no greater joy than to hear that my children are walking in the truth. (1:4).
Beloved, you are faithful in what you are doing for the brothers, and especially since they are strangers to you. (1:5).
They have testified to the church about your love. You will do well to send them on their way in a manner worthy of God. (1:6).
For they went out on behalf of the Name, accepting nothing from the Gentiles. (1:7).
Therefore we ought to support such men, so that we may be fellow workers for the truth. (1:8).
I have written to the church about this, but Diotrephes, who loves to be first, will not accept our instruction. (1:9).

So if I come, I will call attention to his malicious slander against us. And unsatisfied with that, he refuses to welcome the brothers and forbids those who want to do so, even putting them out of the church. (1:10).
Beloved, do not imitate what is evil, but what is good. The one who does good is of God; the one who does evil has not seen God. (1:11).
Demetrius has received a good testimony from everyone, and from the truth itself. We also testify for him, and you know that our testimony is true. (1:12).
I have many things to write to you, but I would prefer not to do so with pen and ink. (1:13).
Instead, I hope to see you soon and speak with you face to face. (1:14).
Peace to you. The friends here send you greetings. Greet each of our friends there by name. (1:15).
crossRefs: Romans 12:13: Contribute to the needs of the saints, practice hospitality.
Matthew 10:40–42: Whoever receives you receives me.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הֹלֵךְ בֶּאֱמֶת (hōlēḵ beʾĕmeṯ), Greek: περιπατοῦντα ἐν τῇ ἀληθείᾳ (peripatounta en tē alētheía, NT), Aramaic: מהלך בקושטא (mehaleḵ b-quštā)
translationNotes.note: Biblical idiom meaning to live one’s life in alignment with God’s truth, showing both belief and conduct.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הַכְנָסַת אוֹרְחִים (hakhnāsat ʾōrḥîm, sense), Greek: φιλοξενία (philoxenía, NT), Aramaic: אושפיזא (ʾūšpīzā)
translationNotes.note: Hospitality was central in early Christian mission, enabling traveling teachers to be received and supported.

stories.keyTakeaway: John commends Gaius for walking in truth and showing faithful hospitality to brothers, urging support for such workers in the gospel.

intro:
3 John was written by John the apostle, again self-identified in verse 1 as "the elder" (Greek ho presbyteros), the same author and the same self-designation as in 2 John. The letter was composed at Ephesus around AD 85-95, during the same general period as 1 John and 2 John and likely sent at the same time as 2 John via the same network of traveling Christian messengers. The letter is addressed to a man named Gaius (verse 1: "The elder to the beloved Gaius, whom I love in truth"), a believer in one of the churches under John's oversight, otherwise unknown outside this letter. Gaius is a common Roman name in the New Testament (other men named Gaius appear in Acts 19:29 as a Macedonian companion of Paul, Acts 20:4 as Gaius of Derbe, and Romans 16:23 / 1 Corinthians 1:14 as Gaius of Corinth in whose house Paul stayed), but none of those Gaiuses can be identified with the recipient of 3 John, who appears to be a different Christian leader living in a city in the Roman province of Asia within John's pastoral reach. For the full biographical sketch of John the apostle (Galilean fisherman, son of Zebedee, brother of James, the inner three, the disciple Jesus loved, caretaker of Mary at the cross, pillar of the Jerusalem church, Ephesian elder, exiled to Patmos under Domitian, died in extreme old age around AD 100 as the only apostle not martyred), see the introduction to the Gospel of John.

The historical setting is the same as 1 John and 2 John: the Roman province of Asia under Domitian (AD 81-96), with John as the senior apostolic voice from Ephesus. The occasion for 3 John is the mirror image of 2 John's concern. Where 2 John warned the elect lady NOT to extend hospitality to false teachers, 3 John commends Gaius for faithfully extending hospitality to true teachers (verses 5-8: "Beloved, it is a faithful thing you do in all your efforts for these brothers, strangers as they are, who testified to your love before the church. You will do well to send them on their journey in a manner worthy of God. For they have gone out for the sake of the name, accepting nothing from the Gentiles. Therefore we ought to support people like these, that we may be fellow workers for the truth"). The traveling missionaries (Greek brothers or adelphoi, perhaps including Demetrius) had passed through Gaius's city carrying out John's apostolic work, had been hosted by Gaius, and had returned to John in Ephesus to report. The letter introduces two figures by name beyond Gaius. The first is Diotrephes (verses 9-10), an ambitious local church leader in a nearby congregation who "likes to put himself first," refused to receive John's letter and the traveling missionaries, slandered John "with wicked nonsense," and went so far as to expel from the church those members who did extend hospitality to John's representatives. Diotrephes's Greek name means "Zeus-nourished," suggesting a Gentile background; he is the only person in the New Testament identified as exercising autocratic control over a local church in opposition to apostolic oversight. The second figure is Demetrius (verse 12), who carries John's strong commendation ("Demetrius has received a good testimony from everyone, and from the truth itself; we also add our testimony, and you know that our testimony is true"); Demetrius is most likely the letter-carrier himself, sent by John to Gaius's city to continue the work that Diotrephes was obstructing, and the letter functions in part as Demetrius's letter of recommendation.

3 John is the sixty-fourth book of the Christian Bible, the twenty-fifth book of the New Testament, and the sixth of the seven General Epistles. At fourteen verses (one chapter), it is tied with 2 John as one of the two shortest books in the New Testament. The earliest surviving manuscripts include Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus (both 4th century AD); Papyrus 74 (P74, 7th century) is another important early witness. The letter is unique in the New Testament for being the only book that addresses by name a specific case of pride and abuse of local church authority by a named individual (Diotrephes), and for being the New Testament's clearest window into the early-church practice of supporting traveling Christian missionaries through household hospitality from city to city; that itinerant missionary economy, in which apostolic representatives like Demetrius would travel "for the sake of the name" without accepting any support from pagans, would shape the geographic spread of the Christian movement across the Roman Empire over the next several centuries. The letter closes with John's intention to visit Gaius and confront Diotrephes in person (verses 13-14: "I had much to write to you, but I would rather not write with pen and ink. I hope to see you soon, and we will talk face to face").
